Library of Hands: Fix the Hands, Not the World Model

Hasaan Ahmad Affiliation: University of the West of England, Bristol, UK Correspondence to: hasaan2.ahmad@live.uwe.ac.uk    Qizhen Ying Affiliation: University of Oxford, Oxford, UK    Yuxuan Sun Affiliation: Imperial College London, London, UK    Tianjin Huang Affiliation: University of Exeter, Exeter, UK    Guangming Wang Affiliation: University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK
Abstract

A world model predicts how a scene changes after an action, and a planner uses it to search for actions that reach a goal. If the camera moves or the controller changes, the same command moves the robot differently: when its commands are turned by 90∘, a frozen planner with the LeWM world model that succeeds in 77.5% of episodes succeeds in only 7.8%. Current fixes retrain the model, need training data, or forget a set-up when it returns. We propose Library of Hands (LoH), a training-free method that keeps the world model frozen and corrects only the map from commands to applied actions, which we call the hand. LoH reads the hand through the frozen model, with no extra sensor: it finds the action that best explains the change between two camera images (a reading). It stores every hand it identifies, so a returning set-up is recognised rather than re-learnt. In closed-loop tests, LoH more than doubles success on three simulated tasks, from 28.6% to 62.3%, and loses only 0.6 percentage points when nothing changes. It also works, unchanged, with two other world models and on two of three models pretrained on real robot data, and its gain grows with the quality of its readings.

Keywords: 
world models, model-based planning, test-time adaptation, system identification, continual learning, robot learning

1 Introduction

A world model can be right about the world and still plan with the wrong actions. Latent world models, which predict in a learned compact representation (a latent space) instead of in pixels, now plan robot actions directly from camera images (Maes et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2025; Assran et al., 2025; Terver et al., 2025). A learned predictor models how the scene evolves in response to an action, and a planner searches for the action sequence whose predicted outcome reaches a goal (Rubinstein, 1999). The predictor implicitly assumes that every action follows the convention of its training data. This assumption fails when the camera is moved or the controller is replaced: the same command then moves the robot in a different direction, by a different magnitude (a changed gain), or only after a delay. The situation resembles a joystick mounted with a 90∘ offset, where a forward command moves the robot to the left. Even when the predictor remains an accurate model of the world, every plan is then expressed in the wrong action convention, and nothing in the model reveals the cause. With the LeWM world model (Maes et al., 2026), a frozen planner succeeds in 77.5% of episodes with its original convention, and in 7.8% when its commands are turned by 90∘.

This happens in real deployments. One model, trained once, is used with many cameras, operators and controllers. V-JEPA 2-AC, the action-conditioned version of the V-JEPA 2 video model (JEPA: joint-embedding predictive architecture), reads its action axes from the camera view, so its authors positioned the camera manually (Assran et al., 2025, Sec. 4.3). The JEPA-WM models (Terver et al., 2025) needed a tuned camera and rescaled actions to move from DROID, a large data set of real robot manipulation (Khazatsky et al., 2024), to RoboCasa, a simulated kitchen (Nasiriany et al., 2024). When we move the camera of V-JEPA 2-AC in RoboCasa, the frame in which it reads the commands turns with the camera, as an offline analysis of 261 views of real robot data suggested (Section 4.4). We call the map from commands to applied actions the hand: not a gripper, but the whole interface between the planner and the motors. In control terms, it is an unknown input map. A new operator, controller gain or delay changes the hand, not the world. A moved camera also changes the images; we treat it as a hand when the model still predicts well from the new view, so that the main mismatch is the frame of the actions (Section 2).

Current fixes change the model, need training, or forget (Table 1). Test-time training changes the weights during deployment (Zhang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b), so a model adapted to one hand is miscalibrated after the next change. Methods trained to recognise the set-up infer it from recent observations (Yang et al., 2026) or assign it to one of a few fixed classes (Anonymous, 2026b), but only within their training distribution. A calibration phase (Assran et al., 2025, App. B.4), or a single retained correction, must restart at every change. None of them exploits a simple property of real laboratories: a laboratory has only a few set-ups, and these recur.

Our idea: fix the hands, not the world model. LoH (Library of Hands) is a small module that needs no training and keeps the world model frozen (Figure 2). It works in two steps. Step 1: read the hand through the frozen model. A model that is right about the world can tell which action moved the world. So we ask the frozen predictor which action best explains the change between two successive camera images, and we compare this action, a reading of the applied action, with the command. The world model itself is the sensor: LoH uses only the inputs of the model (the camera image, and the joint state for the models that take it), and no extra sensor. The predictor also tells us how far to trust each reading. Bayesian model comparison then chooses the map by its exact evidence (the probability of the readings under each candidate map), with no complexity penalty to tune. Step 2: remember the hand. A library stores every hand that LoH identifies. When a set-up comes back, LoH only has to recognise its hand, which takes fewer readings than to identify it again.

We test LoH in closed loop (the robot executes its own plans), with hands that change and come back across episodes. Our contributions are:

  • ⋆\star

    Library of Hands (LoH). A method that reads the applied action through the frozen predictor, weighs each reading by its reliability, chooses a map by exact Bayesian evidence, and stores every identified hand, so that a returning hand is recalled rather than identified again (Section 3).

  • ⋆\star

    Evidence across world models. When hands change and come back, LoH more than doubles the success of a frozen planner and costs little when nothing changes. It works unchanged with three world models (Maes et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2025; Terver et al., 2025) on three simulated tasks, and with two of three models pretrained on real robot data in a simulated kitchen, where a moved camera turns the action frame as a hand does. It also leads test-time training on our schedules (Section 4).

  • ⋆\star

    When and why it works. The quality of the readings, which we can measure before deployment, sets the size of the gain. The gain comes from the readings and the library, not from the rule that picks a hand, as our analysis predicts. The library pays most when a hand takes several readings to identify (Sections 4.3, 4.5 and 4.6).

2 Problem Setting

Planning with a frozen world model.

An encoder (a neural network) turns an image oto_{t} into a latent state ztz_{t}, a vector that summarises the scene. A frozen predictor ff takes ztz_{t} and an action block at∈ℝL×ma_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times m} and predicts the next state, z^t+1=f⁡(zt,at)\hat{z}_{t+1}=f(z_{t},a_{t}). A block is a sequence of L=5L=5 consecutive control steps, each with an mm-dimensional action; the predictor treats the whole block as one transition. The index tt therefore counts blocks, and the index kk below counts control steps. A planner, here the cross-entropy method (CEM), a sampling-based optimiser (Rubinstein, 1999), searches for the command blocks whose predicted states reach a goal state zgz_{g}, the latent state of a goal image.

Hands.

Between the planner and the robot, a hand changes each command before it reaches the motors. In episode ee, step kk applies

uk=Me​ck−de+be,u_{k}=M_{e}\,c_{k-d_{e}}+b_{e}, (1)

where ckc_{k} is the command. The matrix MeM_{e} turns and scales the command (it can also mirror it, or be any linear map), de∈{0,…,5}d_{e}\in\{0,\dots,5\} delays it by ded_{e} control steps, and beb_{e} adds an offset. The robot then clips uku_{k} to its limits. In training, the hand is the identity, so the frozen predictor expects the applied action uu as its input. The robot does not know which hand is active. A hand belongs to the deployment, not to the world: the physics that the predictor learned stays correct, and only the meaning of a command changes. This is our main assumption: after a change, the frozen predictor stays accurate on what the robot observes, and the main mismatch can be written as a transformation of the actions. A new controller gain or delay meets it by construction. A moved camera also changes the images, so it meets the assumption only if the model still predicts well from the new view (Section 4.4 tests this). Hands with a dead band (small commands have no effect) or a saturation (large commands are capped) do not fit Equation 1; they test LoH outside its model.

Task and measures.

The robot plays a sequence of episodes, each with a goal and one hand. Between episodes the hand can change, and hands seen before can come back. The robot must reach each goal with the same frozen model and with no label of the active hand. We measure success in three ways: over all episodes; over the first two episodes after a hand comes back (after returns); and over runs in which the hand never changes (no change). Success is the percentage of episodes that reach the goal, and a difference in success is given in percentage points (pp).

3 Method

Our idea.

LoH uses the frozen world model as a sensor of its own hand. If the predictor ff is right about the world, and an action has a visible effect, then what the robot sees tells us which action reached the robot. We find this action by running ff backwards. Its comparison with the command reveals the hand. LoH trains nothing, and the weights of the world model never change. Figure 2 shows the four stages, and Algorithm 1 gives the loop with every constant.

3.1 Sense: reading the applied action

After each block of L=5L=5 control steps (Section 2), the robot knows the latent state ztz_{t} before the block and the observed state zt+1z_{t+1} after it. The applied action is the action that best explains this change under the frozen predictor:

ut∗=arg​mina⁡∥zt+1−f⁡(zt,a)∥22.u^{*}_{t}=\argmin_{a}\;\lVert z_{t+1}-f(z_{t},a)\rVert_{2}^{2}. (2)

We solve Equation 2 with gradient descent from nine starting points and keep the best one. We use a block only if this action explains it well, that is, if its error is small against the surprise threshold θ\theta of the task, the 95th percentile of the prediction error of the frozen model on data with the unchanged hand (Appendix A). An image shows only the net effect of a block, so the reading is the block sum st=g−1​B​ut∗s_{t}=g^{-1}Bu^{*}_{t}. Here BB adds up the five steps of each action axis, and the gain gg (0.94–1.05 on our simulated tasks) corrects the scale of the inversion. We fit gg once, on 1,200 blocks with the unchanged hand and known actions; no episode with a changed hand and no label is used.

How far to trust a reading.

A reading is only as good as the visible effect of the action. When an action has little visible effect on the next observation, for example because the motion of the robot is blocked or the action saturates, a change of the action changes the predicted state only slightly, and the reading is weak (Section 4.1 gives the cases in our tasks). The Jacobian JtJ_{t} of f⁡(zt,⋅)f(z_{t},\cdot) at ut∗u^{*}_{t}, the matrix of derivatives of the predicted state with respect to the action, measures this effect. With a unit Gaussian prior on the normalised action and a latent noise variance sz=θ/Ds_{z}=\theta/D per dimension (DD is the latent dimension), a Laplace approximation (a Gaussian fitted at the optimum) of Equation 2 gives the uncertainty of the reading,

Σt=sz​(Jt⊤​Jt+sz​I)−1,\Sigma_{t}=s_{z}\left(J_{t}^{\top}J_{t}+s_{z}I\right)^{-1}, (3)

and its covariance Ct=g−2​B​Σt​B⊤C_{t}=g^{-2}B\Sigma_{t}B^{\top} (MacKay, 1992b). A flat Jacobian gives a wide covariance, so the reading counts for little. The map fit uses the shape of CtC_{t} as the noise of each reading.

3.2 Explain: choosing a map

Next, LoH explains the readings with a map. For a delay dd, let c¯t(d)=∑i=04c5​t+i−d\bar{c}_{t}^{(d)}=\sum_{i=0}^{4}c_{5t+i-d} be the sum of the commands that block tt applies under this delay. A map predicts the reading as st=M​c¯t(d)+5​b+εts_{t}=M\bar{c}_{t}^{(d)}+5b+\varepsilon_{t} (the offset acts at each of the five steps), with the noise εt∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​R~t)\varepsilon_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}\tilde{R}_{t}) and R~t\tilde{R}_{t} the shape of CtC_{t} (that is, CtC_{t} up to a scale). We compare five classes of map (the number of parameters in parentheses): identity (0); turn and scale γ​R​(ϕ)\gamma R(\phi), a rotation by the angle ϕ\phi with the gain γ\gamma (2); mirror (2); linear (4); and affine, a linear map with an offset (6). A class is a form of map, not a hand: turn and scale alone holds every turn and gain. Each class has six delays d∈{0,…,5}d\in\{0,\dots,5\}, so there are 30 models in all. The identity with no delay has the prior probability 0.50.5. A conjugate prior, centred on the identity, gives each model a closed-form evidence, the probability of the readings under the model (MacKay, 1992a; Kass & Raftery, 1995). The evidence is exact, so there is no complexity penalty to tune.

Actuator limits.

A physical actuator has a limited range, so many robots clip each applied action to a fixed interval, for example [−1,1][-1,1]. A clipped action moves the robot less than the linear map predicts, so a map fitted to the raw commands underestimates the gain. A gain above 1 cannot be observed when the actions saturate, so we limit the current map to a largest singular value (its largest gain in any direction) of 1, T=M^/max⁡(1,σmax​(M^))T=\hat{M}/\max(1,\sigma_{\max}(\hat{M})). The effective commands c~=T−1​(clip⁡(T​c+b)−b)\tilde{c}=T^{-1}(\mathrm{clip}(Tc+b)-b) then make the linear model exact, and a fixed-point iteration refits the map on them.

3.3 Remember: a library of hands

A stored hand is easier to recognise than a new hand is to identify. The library has no fixed list of hands: it keeps the map of every hand seen so far. In each episode, several sources compete to explain the readings 𝒟\mathcal{D} of the current segment (the blocks since the start of the episode or the last detected switch): each stored hand kk, and a “new” source that fits a map from 𝒟\mathcal{D} alone. A stored hand scores 𝒟\mathcal{D} with its own posterior over the 30 models as the prior. So a stored hand needs only enough readings to be recognised, while a new hand must be identified.

Which hand to expect.

Hands usually stay, so the prior over the sources favours the hand of the previous episode (a sticky prior). That hand gets 1−h1-h, the new source gets h​qhq, and the other stored hands share h⁡(1−q)h(1-q) in proportion to their use. The switch rate hh and the new-hand rate qq are learned from the last 20 events. The planner uses the most probable model of the source with the most posterior mass.

Keeping the library clean.

Inside an episode, the last four blocks are also scored alone, so a switch in the middle of an episode can start a new segment. At the end of an episode, a segment creates a new hand only if the new source explains it best and the segment has at least four blocks. Otherwise, only the hands that won the segment learn from its blocks, so the data of one hand do not overwrite another. Two hands merge when the evidence favours one hand over two, and unused hands fade (Appendix A). A map with a smallest singular value below 0.2 (the weakest hand has gain 0.5) says that the commands have no effect: an obstruction or a lost reading, not a hand. The planner never uses it, and no segment that it explains best is stored (Section C.3).

3.4 Act: planning through the map

CEM samples command blocks, keeps the best ones (the elites) and refits its sampling distribution to them (300 samples, 30 iterations, 30 elites, a horizon of five blocks). Before the frozen model predicts the outcome of a candidate, LoH passes it through the chosen map, delay and clip. The frozen model therefore sees the actions that will really reach the robot. The cost is the squared distance from the final state to the goal. The robot replans at once when the one-block prediction error exceeds the surprise threshold θ\theta (Section 3.1), and otherwise after five blocks.

3.5 What the theory predicts

We analyse LoH as Bayesian regression of the readings on the commands (Appendix B). We write 𝔼⁡[st]=Xt​β\mathbb{E}[s_{t}]=X_{t}\beta, where β\beta holds the parameters of a map and XtX_{t} is linear in c¯t(d)\bar{c}_{t}^{(d)}.

Proposition 3.1 (Identifiability (Informal)).

For a fixed class and delay, nn readings identify a map if and only if the reliability-weighted Fisher information ℐn=σ−2​∑t≤nXt⊤​R~t−1​Xt\mathcal{I}_{n}=\sigma^{-2}\sum_{t\leq n}X_{t}^{\top}\tilde{R}_{t}^{-1}X_{t} is nonsingular (invertible). One block with c¯t(d)≠0\bar{c}_{t}^{(d)}\neq 0 identifies a turn with a gain, or a mirror.

A tracking bound (Proposition B.4, Corollary B.5) adds that the library pays only a few nats (units of log-evidence) at each switch, so selection rules that differ in this prior, such as Fixed Share, an algorithm that tracks the best of several predictors over time (Herbster & Warmuth, 1998), and the cumulative-sum (CUSUM) change detector (Page, 1954), choose almost the same hand (Section 4.6), and every rule plans the first block after a switch with the previous hand.

Lemma B.6 explains the false alarms when nothing changes, and Proposition B.3 shows that identifying a delay requires, in general, one more block of readings than identifying the map alone. Of 24 testable predictions, 16 hold on the logs of the final method (Table 10).

4 Experiments

Our experiments address four questions. (i) Does LoH recover the success lost to a changed hand, without a loss when the hand does not change (Section 4.2)? (ii) Does it transfer to other world models (Section 4.3)? (iii) Why does it work: does the gain follow the quality of the sensor (Section 4.5), and which component of LoH produces it (Section 4.6)? (iv) Does it outperform learned and calibration methods, and a planner with a larger search budget (Section 4.7)?

4.1 Experimental Setup

World models and tasks.

Our main world model is LeWM (LeWorldModel; Maes et al., 2026), a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) trained from pixels, with its released checkpoints (trained weights) for three simulated control tasks. In PushT (Florence et al., 2021; Chi et al., 2023), a circular pusher pushes a T-shaped block to a target position and angle. In Reacher (Tassa et al., 2018), a planar arm with two joints moves to a target joint configuration. In Two-Room (Sobal et al., 2025), a point agent moves to a target in a plane that a wall with a door divides into two rooms. In all three tasks, the action is 2-D and the world model observes the scene through images (Table 7). To test whether LoH depends on LeWM, we also run two other world models on the same three tasks. DINO-WM (Zhou et al., 2025) adds action features to the frozen features of DINOv2, a pretrained image encoder (Oquab et al., 2024). JEPA-WM (Terver et al., 2025) feeds the action through adaptive layer normalisation. On PushT we use their released checkpoints and data. Reacher and Two-Room have no released checkpoints, so we train both models on the data of LeWM with their authors’ recipes (one run each). A small adapter gives each model the interface of LeWM. The method code does not change. In these tasks, readings are weak when the agent pushes against a wall (Two-Room) and when an action is clipped at the actuator limits (Reacher and Two-Room clip each applied action to [−1,1][-1,1]). Without the clip model of Section 3.2, the stored map of the unchanged hand on Two-Room had a gain of 0.70 instead of 1. Cube, in which a simulated 3-D robot arm with 5-D actions moves a cube, is a further test (Section 6).

Choice of hands.

The hands are test conditions; LoH is not given a list of them. Each hand changes one term of Equation 1, as a real change of set-up does (Table 2), so that each result can be attributed to that term. Each value also tests a different part of LoH. Under the turn of 90∘, the frozen planner almost always fails (7.8%; Table 12), so hand A shows the full loss. The turn of 37∘ is not a multiple of 45∘, so a choice among a few fixed turns cannot express it. No turn can express the mirror, so it needs its own class of map. Hand C combines a gain with a delay, so the map fit must also find the delay. The random turns T are new hands that no list contains. They are drawn from the whole range [−90∘,90∘][-90^{\circ},90^{\circ}], so the gain does not rest on the value 37∘: on them, LoH raises success from 28.6% to 57.0% (Table 12). The offset bb translates the applied action: at every step, the robot moves by an additional constant displacement, as with an actuator bias or a miscalibrated zero. We evaluate the offset on a separate schedule (Section 4.7). Hands outside Equation 1, with dead bands and saturation, evaluate LoH beyond its model.

Schedules.

A schedule sets the hand of every episode, and a return is a switch back to a hand that was already active earlier in the run. Each schedule has 140 episodes and tests one situation. In S1 (fixed returns), hands return in a fixed, predetermined order: the schedule cycles through A, C, A, C, D, A, D, and each hand stays for five consecutive episodes. S1 thus mixes the first visits of three hands with their returns at known times, so it shows recall visit by visit (Figure 3). In S2 (random returns), the last hand stays with probability 0.6. Otherwise, the schedule draws a new turn in [−90∘,90∘][-90^{\circ},90^{\circ}] with probability 0.1, and else one of A, C, D, E, N with equal probability. Hands thus return at random times and new hands appear, so neither the order nor the set of hands is known in advance. S3 (no returns) applies a new turn in every episode: there is nothing to recall, so S3 measures the identification of new hands alone. S4 (60 episodes) never changes the hand, and it measures the cost of LoH when nothing changes. The after returns measure is the success in the first two episodes after each return (the switch episode and the next one), pooled over S1 and S2.

Baselines.

We compare LoH with nine baselines in three groups. Simple: (1) the frozen planner; (2) identification in every episode, with no memory; (3) one memory, which keeps only the last map. Hand trackers: (4) Fixed Share over the same library (Herbster & Warmuth, 1998); (5) a change detector in the style of MBCD (Alegre et al., 2021), which switches between stored models with a CUSUM test; (6) a method in the style of ShiftWM-Bench (Anonymous, 2026b), which assigns the change to one of a few fixed classes, with no memory. Adaptation and search: (7) test-time training of the action encoder of the world model, and AdaJEPA, an adaptive latent world model (Wang et al., 2026b); (8) a calibration at the start of every episode (Assran et al., 2025, App. B.4); (9) the frozen planner with two and four times more CEM iterations. Baselines (5)–(8) are our re-implementations. Two oracles, which receive privileged information, mark the ceiling: one plans with the true hand, and one is told which hand is active but fits its map with the sensor of LoH.

Protocol.

We evaluate all methods with fixed protocols and report paired bootstrap confidence intervals across runs. A run is one task, seed and schedule, and all methods play the same episodes. We give each paired difference as its mean over runs, with its 95% bootstrap confidence interval (CI) in square brackets. The main comparison, the locked test, uses 20 new seeds and sign-flip permutation tests with Holm’s correction over its eight comparisons (Appendix A). Each test has a pass threshold (a bar) that we fixed before its runs; Appendix D gives every verdict and the development history of the method. All results of LoH use the final method of Section 3, with the floor of Section 3.3; LoH without the floor is an ablation (Section 4.6).

4.2 LoH Recalls Returning Hands

Table 3 gives the locked test. ❶ LoH more than doubles the success of the frozen planner. Over all episodes, success rises from 28.6% to 62.3%. On the 12 seeds on which we also ran the true hand, LoH closes 69.2% of the gap to it (frozen planner 28.4%, LoH 62.4%, true hand 77.5%). After returns, LoH is on average 33.9 pp above the frozen planner (95% CI [31.1, 36.6]). ❷ LoH beats every baseline. It is best on every task over all episodes, and after returns it leads Fixed Share by 5.5 pp and the MBCD-style detector by 8.4. It leads one memory by 15.5 and the ShiftWM-style method by 24.6 (all Holm-corrected p<0.001p<0.001; Appendix C). ❸ It costs little when nothing changes. With no change, LoH loses 0.6 pp [−0.9-0.9, −0.2-0.2]. This loss is statistically significant (Holm-corrected p=0.003p=0.003) but small. In 95.4% of the S4 episodes, every plan uses the exact identity; false alarms in the other episodes cause almost all of the loss.

Figure 3 shows how the library makes this gain on S1. At the first visit of a hand, LoH must identify it (59.2%, against 76.4% for the true hand). When the hand returns, the library recalls it (70.5% against 76.9% over the 25 returns). In the second episode after a return, LoH matches the true hand (75.3% against 78.5%) and leads one memory by 14.3 pp. One memory with the same sensor must identify the hand again after each switch and needs about four episodes (63.0% over the returns; no memory: 42.4%).

4.3 One Method, Three World Models

Table 4 runs the same method on two other world models, which feed the action into the predictor in different ways, on the same three tasks; Figure 1 gives the share of the gap closed in each cell (one world model on one task). ❶ Both read their own actions well (sensor R2R^{2} 0.93–0.998; without the joint-state (proprioceptive) input, 0.87–0.88 on Reacher; Appendix A). ❷ LoH gains in every cell. After returns, it is 31.3 to 64.6 pp above the frozen planner on S1 and 26.3 to 63.1 on S2, where hands come back at random. With no change, it stays within 2 pp of the frozen planner in eight of the nine cells; on DINO-WM Reacher it loses 2.5 pp [−7.5-7.5, +2.5+2.5]. ❸ The library pays most when a hand is slow to identify. Recall saves the readings that a fresh fit needs, so its value depends on how many readings identify a hand. On S1, the library leads one memory with the same sensor by 10.0 to 17.3 pp on LeWM, whose readings are less accurate (R2R^{2} 0.70–0.98). On DINO-WM and JEPA-WM (R2R^{2} 0.93–0.998), one memory is close in five of six cells (−8.3-8.3 to +6.2+6.2 pp): one accurate block identifies a hand again, so recall saves little. Over the nine cells, the lead of the library falls as the R2R^{2} of the sensor rises (Spearman ρ=−0.89\rho=-0.89 on S1 and −0.72-0.72 on S2; post hoc). In RoboCasa, a fresh fit is confident by the third of 12 plans, so recall also saves little there (Section 4.4). Very noisy readings, in turn, spoil the stored maps (Section 4.5). The library is thus most useful when a hand takes several readings to identify, and each reading is still accurate enough to store a correct map. On S2, where new hands also appear, it leads in four of six cells (5.5 to 11.5 pp, 95% interval above 0).

4.4 World Models Pretrained on Real Robot Data

We test LoH on the three world models that Terver et al. (2025) pretrained on real robot data (Khazatsky et al., 2024): DINO-WM, JEPA-WM and V-JEPA 2-AC. Each plans in RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024), a simulated 3-D kitchen, with its released planner unchanged, and the hand acts on the commands of the end effector (the gripper). An admission test (a turn of 90∘ must cost the frozen planner 15 pp) admits the place task, in which the robot puts an object at a target, for all three models; we do not run the reach task, where the frozen planner rarely succeeds even with the true hand. Schedule S1 runs 35 episodes in blocks of five, and the success criteria are those of the simulated tasks (Section C.5).

On DINO-WM, LoH lifts success after returns from 7.8% to 26.6% (Figure 4), does not lose when nothing changes, and over all 35 episodes equals the planner told the hand (30.7% and 30.4%). On S2 (random returns), it gains 11.4 pp [5.3, 17.1]. On V-JEPA 2-AC, it gains 14.1 pp after returns, with a wide interval ([−3.1-3.1, +29.7+29.7]), and equals the planner told the hand (35.9%). On JEPA-WM, it gains only 7.8 pp [3.1, 10.9] and costs 6.2 pp with no change. LoH thus works on two of the three models (Section C.5 gives the criteria). Each model reads the RoboCasa commands in a frame turned by 22 to 39∘, which follows the camera: a camera move by θ\theta turns it by −0.68​θ-0.68\,\theta on DINO-WM and −0.85​θ-0.85\,\theta on V-JEPA 2-AC over all camera yaw angles, near the slope of −0.67-0.67 that it showed offline on DROID images (Figure 7). A camera move thus turns the frame as a hand does (the test fails on JEPA-WM; Section C.5). LoH removes this turn with the injected hand, so it can equal the planner told the hand. LoH recalls a returning hand at its first plan in 27 to 38% of the returns; its lead over one memory (−3.1-3.1 to +4.7+4.7 pp) is not significant: a fresh fit is confident by plan 3 of 12, so recall saves little (post hoc).

4.5 The Quality of the Sensor Sets the Gain

LoH rests on one claim: the frozen model is a sensor of its own hand. If this is true, a worse sensor must give a smaller gain. We add Gaussian noise to each reading, with a standard deviation of σ\sigma times the standard deviation of the commands, add its variance to the reliability of the reading, and change nothing else. The gain over the frozen planner falls at every step: on LeWM from 43.6 to 1.4 pp on PushT and Reacher and from 18.2 to −3.2-3.2 on Two-Room, and on DINO-WM from 58.3 to 10.4 (Figure 5a). All three tests of this fall pass. Across models and noise levels, the share of the possible gain that LoH captures rises with the measured quality of the sensor (Figure 5b; Spearman rank correlation ρ=0.91\rho=0.91, 18 data points). A fourth test fails: the advantage of the library over no memory does not grow with the noise (+0.2+0.2 [−3.9-3.9, +4.4+4.4]), because noisy readings spoil stored maps. The value of the library thus peaks at an intermediate quality of the readings: on PushT, the task with the most accurate readings, it is largest at σ=0.6\sigma=0.6; on Two-Room, at σ=0.3\sigma=0.3; on Reacher, the least accurate, it only falls (Table 15; point estimates, post hoc).

4.6 Where the Gain Comes From

The gain should come from the sensor, the choice of map and the library. The baselines marked †\dagger in Table 3 use an earlier sensor: a manually tuned motion threshold, no reliability weights and no clip model. Their gap thus mixes the sensor and the library. Figure 6 therefore removes one stage of Figure 2 at a time (per task: Table 13).

  • •

    Sense. The full sensor adds 5.9 pp [3.9, 7.8] with the sticky prior and 6.2 pp [3.9, 8.6] with Fixed Share. Noise on the readings removes almost the whole gain (Section 4.5).

  • •

    Explain. One fixed linear map costs 9.1 pp [6.9, 11.4]. No delay search costs 6.1 pp [3.6, 8.5], and 25.1 [20.6, 29.6] on the delayed hand C.

  • •

    Remember. With the same sensor, LoH is 16.6 pp [13.5, 19.7] above no memory and 12.3 pp [10.1, 14.5] above one memory.

  • •

    The floor. On the locked test, LoH without the floor is within 0.4 pp of LoH (S1–S3: −0.4-0.4 [−0.9-0.9, +0.1+0.1]). The floor matters in long runs: in the 500-episode streams of Section 4.7 on PushT with no change, the library without it stores maps under which the commands have no effect, and its AUC falls from 82.5 to 52.9 (frozen planner: 83.3; Section C.3).

  • •

    Act. Without a map in the plan, only the frozen planner remains: 35.1 pp [30.6, 39.6] below LoH, and 33.9 [31.1, 36.6] on all 20 seeds of the locked test.

  • •

    The rule that picks a hand matters little. With the same sensor and library, the sticky prior ties with Fixed Share (−0.9-0.9 [−2.7-2.7, +0.9+0.9]), as Section 3.5 predicts, and is 2.7 pp [0.9, 4.5] above CUSUM. The +5.5+5.5 over Fixed Share in Table 3 comes from the sensor, so we do not claim the rule.

  • •

    Recognition is the remaining gap. An oracle that is told the hand, with the same sensor, is 15.3 pp [13.2, 17.3] higher after returns. The gap is the first block after a switch, planned with the previous hand. A cue from the first image of an episode closes about 40% of this gap (+6.0+6.0 [4.0, 8.2]; Table 14).

4.7 Comparison with Alternatives and Compute

Test-time training.

On the protocol and the eight dynamics shifts of JEPA-TTT (Zhang et al., 2026), a test-time training method for latent world models (streams of 500 episodes; Section C.4), LoH leads JEPA-TTT by 14.3 pp of best success on the action rotation and by 2.8 pp of the area under the success curve (AUC) over six shifts. It loses on Two-Room, where the turn depends on the position. With no change, it stays within 1 pp of the frozen planner, while JEPA-TTT loses up to 11. In our schedules, continual test-time training, AdaJEPA (Wang et al., 2026b), JEPA-TTT and a calibration in every episode (Assran et al., 2025, App. B.4) are 34.1, 33.7, 33.8 and 18.4 pp below LoH after returns.

The gain is not extra compute.

A correct map causes fewer surprises, so LoH replans about half as often and uses 0.78–0.82 times the GPU time per step of the frozen planner. More search does not help: with four times the CEM iterations, the frozen planner costs 3.6–4.2 times as much per step, loses 2.6 pp [0.6, 4.9] after returns, and stays 36.1 pp [31.0, 41.2] below LoH (Section C.4).

Further results (Table 14).

With 2, 4 and 8 recurring hands, LoH is 4.4, 4.8 and 6.9 pp above one memory (same sensor); with 16 and 24, 8.1 and 4.2, and it ties Fixed Share; fresh seeds and Two-Room give the same verdicts. Over 400 episodes, success does not decay (−2.8-2.8 [−8.5-8.5, +3.1+3.1]). On hands with dead bands and saturations, which a linear map cannot express, LoH is still 15.9 pp [14.0, 17.7] above the frozen planner. An offset bb costs the frozen planner 41.8 pp, and LoH wins back 23.4 [14.0, 32.6]; on Two-Room, where it costs 3.1, LoH is 6.2 below it, mostly in the first episode after a switch (post hoc). A partial run on DINO-WM and JEPA-WM points the same way, with no verdict. With one hand for 140 episodes, LoH equals the true hand (−0.3-0.3 pp).

5 Related Work

Latent world models and the meaning of an action.

Latent world models plan from pixels by searching through a learned predictor (Maes et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2025; Assran et al., 2025; Sobal et al., 2025; Zholus et al., 2026). Latent actions are relative to the camera (Garrido et al., 2026), and calibrated methods draw the robot axes into the image with known camera poses (Jang et al., 2026). We instead treat the hand as a property of the deployment and identify it through the released model.

Test-time adaptation and trained identification.

Test-time training changes the weights during deployment (Sun et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b). Sandwich-Residuals fits a residual on the action embedding in each episode (Soni et al., 2026), and RWM, which uses a world model as a reference trajectory, trains a residual controller online (Brito & McNamee, 2025). Methods trained to recognise the set-up infer it from recent observations: with context encoders (Kumar et al., 2021), in-context world models (Yang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a), or a meta-learned belief through a frozen dynamics model (Li et al., 2026). The closest work, ShiftWM-Bench (Anonymous, 2026b), uses the same frozen LeWM and tasks. It trains an ensemble that sorts residuals into three or four fixed classes, with no memory across episodes. Our 90∘ and mirror hands lie outside all of these classes. LoH instead estimates a continuous map through the released model and keeps it across episodes.

Inversion, action grounding and adaptive control.

V-JEPA 2 inverts its frozen predictor on a random trajectory to fit a 2×22\times 2 map offline, as a calibration phase that its experiments do not use (Assran et al., 2025, App. B.4). AIME (action inference by maximising evidence) infers actions under a frozen world model for imitation (Zhang et al., 2023). Grounded action transformation (Hanna & Stone, 2017), disturbance observers and L1 adaptive control (Hovakimyan & Cao, 2010) correct the input of a fixed model. Multiple-model adaptive control and SpikeWorld choose among fixed models (Athans et al., 1977; Yu, 2026). ECA (efference-copy adaptation) identifies and inverts an actuator map (ordering, direction and gain) from the error of a frozen forward model, for policies on states, and withdraws when the identity or a delayed identity explains the data better (Li & Liu, 2026). We identify the map online through a frozen pixel world model.

Libraries of models and tracking.

In motor control, MOSAIC, a set of paired forward and inverse models (Wolpert & Kawato, 1998), and COIN, a model of contextual inference (Heald et al., 2021), infer the context over a set of motor memories, also from a cue before the movement. In model-based reinforcement learning, growing sets of dynamics models with a sticky or Chinese-restaurant prior appear in Xu et al. (2020), in meta-learned online adaptation (MOLe; Nagabandi et al., 2019), in lifelong incremental reinforcement learning (LLIRL; Wang et al., 2022) and in change-point detection for non-stationary reinforcement learning (MBCD; Alegre et al., 2021). Anonymous (2026a) analyse first visits and revisits of recurring dynamics. Choosing a stored hand is tracking the best expert. Fixed Share pays the identification cost in every segment (Herbster & Warmuth, 1998), and Mixing Past Posteriors pays it once for each distinct expert (Bousquet & Warmuth, 2002; Koolen et al., 2012). Change-point methods detect switches (Page, 1954; Adams & MacKay, 2007).

6 Limitations and Discussion

Switches inside an episode.

When the hand changes in the middle of an episode, LoH has a mean gain of 6.6 pp (95% CI [4.2, 9.4]), below its bar of 10 pp. On new seeds, the mean gain is 9.9 pp (95% CI [8.0, 11.8]). It replans only after a surprise, so it reads the new hand late.

The blind first block.

Every rule plans the first block of an episode with the previous hand. When the hand goes back to “no change”, this costs 9.4 pp [7.2, 11.4] against the frozen planner (S2, post hoc). After 120 episodes of one hand, nearly all the loss is this episode. It is the recognition gap of Section 4.6, which a cue from the first image of an episode reduces.

Changes of the world.

When the world changes and the hand does not (the friction or the centre of gravity of the PushT block), LoH loses 5.0 pp [3.2, 7.1], so the bar of −3-3 failed. The change adds scatter to the readings, and model selection sometimes accepts a false map.

When the planner is the limit.

On Cube, the true hand is only 12 pp above the frozen planner, and LoH closes half of this gap; two of the three bars fail (Appendix C).

The frame of a real-data model.

The models pretrained on real robot data read the RoboCasa commands in a frame that follows the camera on two of three models (Section 4.4). Our sensor removes only the gain, so LoH learns the turn as a permanent hand; a sensor that removes the full calibrated map is the next step. Behind the robot, outside the DROID cameras, the sensor reads little: there, the change of view breaks our assumption that the model stays accurate (Section 2). Our other hands are injected, and a comparison with models trained on randomised interfaces (Yang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a) remains open.

Toward robots.

The library has no fixed list of hands: it adds an entry for each new hand, and we test it with up to 24. Its five classes of map are fixed, however, so it cannot express a kind of hand outside them. A real robot needs more. The first step is a module that discovers new kinds of hand online, such as hands that change with the state (the Two-Room loss of Section C.4). The others are harder and longer tasks (Liu et al., 2023), other robot bodies, and a test on a real robot.

7 Conclusion

LoH fixes the hands, not the world model. In closed-loop tests, it more than doubles the success of a frozen planner when hands change and come back, costs 0.6 pp when they do not, and works unchanged on three world models and on two of three models pretrained on real robot data. The quality of the sensor sets the size of the gain: the frozen model keeps the physics, and a small map read through it keeps the interface.

Appendix A Protocol

Algorithm 1 gives the loop of LoH in one episode, and Table 6 gives its constants. The constants of the library are the same in every cell. Each task calibrates only the surprise threshold θ\theta and the gain gg, on unshifted data.

World models and tasks.

LeWM (Maes et al., 2026) uses a ViT-tiny encoder, a 192-dimensional latent, a predictor with 6 layers and a history of 3 frames. One model step is a block of 5 environment steps. Each task starts from a random state of a random expert episode, and the goal is the state 25 environment steps later in that episode. Episode ii of seed ss has the same start, goal, random seeds and hand in every arm. Each episode has 50 environment steps (Two-Room: 25, where the planner has no headroom at 50). Table 7 gives the tasks.

DINO-WM and JEPA-WM.

An adapter gives each model the interface of LeWM, and the method code does not change. The state is the vector of visual and proprioceptive features, scaled so that squared distance equals the planning cost of the model. Reacher and Two-Room have no public checkpoints, so we trained each model once on the data of LeWM, with the recipe of its authors and a 90/10 split by episode. These models take the proprioceptive state as an input, so their high sensor R2R^{2} could come from the joint state. We repeated each calibration with the inversion energy restricted to the visual part of the state. The reading was fixed in advance: R2≥0.90R^{2}\geq 0.90 keeps the claim that the model reads its actions from images. On PushT and Two-Room, the masked R2R^{2} is 0.93–0.99, so the claim holds. On Reacher, it is 0.87–0.88, so part of the reading there comes from the joint state.

Further hands and schedules.

Table 2 gives the main hands, and Table 8 gives the others. The parts of a hand act in a fixed order: latency, mirror, rotation, gain, dead band, saturation, offset, then the clip of the environment. Table 9 gives the schedules. A return is a switch to a hand that occurred earlier in the run. After returns counts the switch episode and the next episode if the hand stays, and pools S1 and S2.

Arms.

The frozen planner runs CEM on the frozen model with the identity map. The true-hand arm plans through the full chain of the true hand. The earlier sensor (†) has no Laplace reliability, no clip model and a gain of 1. No memory† identifies the hand in each episode, and one memory† keeps one memory of 64 blocks. Fixed Share† uses the same library with a motion gate and a prior of 0.8 on the last hand (Herbster & Warmuth, 1998). MBCD-style† uses a CUSUM selector that switches at 3 nats (Alegre et al., 2021; Page, 1954). ShiftWM-style scores seven fixed hypotheses by exact evidence, with no memory (Anonymous, 2026b). Same-sensor arms give these comparisons the full sensor of LoH. Continual test-time training takes one Adam step (learning rate 10−410^{-4}) on a copy of the action encoder after each transition (Zhang et al., 2026). The calibration arm adds a random excitation block at the start of every episode. More search uses 60 or 120 CEM iterations.

Statistics.

The unit is the run. For each run, we take the mean success of one arm minus another over the episodes of the measure. The bootstrap resamples the run-level differences 20,000 times, and the sign-flip test uses 20,000 sign vectors. Holm’s correction covers the eight comparisons of the locked rules. All other rules are bars on the estimate or on the interval, with no correction for multiplicity. Development used 69 seeds. The locked test uses 20 further seeds, and the true-hand arm ran on 12 of them; paired comparisons with it use only these 12 seeds. Later tests use the locked-test seeds or fresh seeds; some of these sets reuse task lists on other schedules or arms. Reacher runs do not repeat bit for bit across GPU nodes because of the MuJoCo rendering, so all comparisons are paired within one set of runs. GPU ratios come from shared GPUs and are approximate.

Appendix B Theory

We analyse LoH as Bayesian regression of the readings on the commands. This appendix states the main results with proof sketches. All logarithms are natural.

Model.

Block tt covers L=5L=5 steps, and ck=0c_{k}=0 for k<0k<0. A hand applies uk=clip⁡(M​ck−d+b)u_{k}=\operatorname{clip}(Mc_{k-d}+b). The commanded window sum is c¯t(d)=∑i=0L−1cL​t+i−d\bar{c}_{t}^{(d)}=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}c_{Lt+i-d}. Given a model h=(class,d)h=(\text{class},d), the reading is st=Xt​β+εts_{t}=X_{t}\beta+\varepsilon_{t} with εt∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​R~t)\varepsilon_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}\tilde{R}_{t}). With QQ the turn by 90∘90^{\circ} and F=diag⁡(−1,1)F=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1), the designs are [c¯t,Q​c¯t][\bar{c}_{t},Q\bar{c}_{t}] (similarity), [F​c¯t,Q​F​c¯t][F\bar{c}_{t},QF\bar{c}_{t}] (reflection), c¯t⊤⊗I2\bar{c}_{t}^{\top}\otimes I_{2} (linear) and [c¯t⊤⊗I2,I2][\bar{c}_{t}^{\top}\otimes I_{2},I_{2}] (affine). The prior is normal-inverse-gamma, so each model has a closed-form evidence Z⁡(𝒟∣h)Z(\mathcal{D}\mid h) (MacKay, 1992a). A stored entry ℓ\ell uses its own map posterior as the prior of the map. The prior over sources for episode ee is

πe​(last)=1−ρe,πe​(new)=ρe​ξe,πe​(ℓ)=ρe​(1−ξe)​Uℓ∑j≠lastUj,\pi_{e}(\text{last})=1-\rho_{e},\qquad\pi_{e}(\text{new})=\rho_{e}\xi_{e},\qquad\pi_{e}(\ell)=\rho_{e}(1-\xi_{e})\,\frac{U_{\ell}}{\sum_{j\neq\text{last}}U_{j}}, (4)

where ρe\rho_{e} and ξe\xi_{e} are the rates hh and qq of the main text, and the use counts follow Uℓ←γ⁡(Uℓ+rℓ)U_{\ell}\leftarrow\gamma(U_{\ell}+r_{\ell}) with γ=0.98\gamma=0.98.

Assumptions.

A1: no applied step reaches the clip, or the clip model is at its fixed point with T=MT=M and σmax​(M)≤1\sigma_{\max}(M)\leq 1. A2: given the past and c¯t\bar{c}_{t}, 𝔼⁡[st]=Xt​β\mathbb{E}[s_{t}]=X_{t}\beta and Cov⁡(st)=σ2​R~t\operatorname{Cov}(s_{t})=\sigma^{2}\tilde{R}_{t}. A3: the errors are independent across blocks given the past, and commands may depend on past readings. A4: in the Fisher statements, σ2\sigma^{2} is known. For tracking: T1: the hand switches only between episodes. T2: the comparator is a label oracle with the fits of the method, with loss Llabel′L^{\prime}_{\text{label}}. T3: each earlier hand has exactly one entry, which holds all its past blocks and no other block. T4: the prior over sources is fixed before the episode. On the logs, A2 holds for the typical block and fails in the tails (the kurtosis of the whitened residuals is 152 on PushT), and T3 holds only in part.

Proposition B.1 (Identifiability of the map).

Fix the class and the delay, and let ℐn=σ−2​∑t≤nXt⊤​R~t−1​Xt\mathcal{I}_{n}=\sigma^{-2}\sum_{t\leq n}X_{t}^{\top}\tilde{R}_{t}^{-1}X_{t}. Under A1–A4:

  1. (a)

    β\beta is identifiable from s1:ns_{1:n} if and only if ℐn\mathcal{I}_{n} is nonsingular.

  2. (b)

    One block with c¯t≠0\bar{c}_{t}\neq 0 identifies a similarity or a reflection. A linear map needs two window sums that are not parallel, and an affine map three that are not on one line.

  3. (c)

    The posterior and the evidence keep their form when c¯t\bar{c}_{t} depends on s1:t−1s_{1:t-1}.

Sketch.

The log-likelihood is quadratic in β\beta with Hessian −ℐn-\mathcal{I}_{n}. Two values give the same distribution if and only if Xt​(β−β′)=0X_{t}(\beta-\beta^{\prime})=0 for all tt, which is (β−β′)⊤​ℐn​(β−β′)=0(\beta-\beta^{\prime})^{\top}\mathcal{I}_{n}(\beta-\beta^{\prime})=0, because the eigenvalues of R~t\tilde{R}_{t} are bounded; the model is linear in β\beta (Rothenberg, 1971). For (b), [c¯,Q​c¯][\bar{c},Q\bar{c}] is ∥c¯∥\lVert\bar{c}\rVert times an orthogonal matrix, and (c¯t⊤,1)(\bar{c}_{t}^{\top},1) must span ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} in the affine class. For (c), the joint density factorises into the block likelihoods and factors free of β\beta and σ2\sigma^{2} (Lai & Wei, 1982). ∎

Proposition B.2 (Clipped actions).

Let c~k=T−1​(clip⁡(T​ck+b)−b)\tilde{c}_{k}=T^{-1}(\operatorname{clip}(Tc_{k}+b)-b) be the effective commands of a transform TT. (a) If MM is invertible, σmax​(M)≤1\sigma_{\max}(M)\leq 1 and T=MT=M, the mean of a reading is exactly M​c~t(d)+L​bM\tilde{c}_{t}^{(d)}+Lb; if σmax​(M)>1\sigma_{\max}(M)>1, this fails on clipped steps. (b) An axis that is clipped at every step of a block gives no information about its row of MM, and a gain above 1 is not identified from saturated commands. (c) R~t\tilde{R}_{t} depends only on the state and on ut∗u_{t}^{*}, so the reliability cannot down-weight a block because it was clipped.

Sketch.

(a) By definition, T​c~k+b=clip⁡(T​ck+b)T\tilde{c}_{k}+b=\operatorname{clip}(Tc_{k}+b); sum over the block. (b) For a fixed clip pattern, the Jacobian of the mean in vec⁡(M)\operatorname{vec}(M) is ∑kck−d⊤⊗Γk\sum_{k}c_{k-d}^{\top}\otimes\Gamma_{k}, where Γk\Gamma_{k} is the diagonal 0/1 matrix of the unclipped axes, so its row for a fully clipped axis is zero. (c) A clipped and an unclipped command with the same applied action give the same JtJ_{t}. ∎

Proposition B.3 (Identification of the delay).

Under A1–A3: (a) for the same invertible map and offset, delays dd and d′d^{\prime} are indistinguishable on a set of blocks if and only if c¯t(d)=c¯t(d′)\bar{c}_{t}^{(d)}=\bar{c}_{t}^{(d^{\prime})} on each block, and in later blocks constant or LL-periodic commands hide the delay; (b) a free map matches any readings on one block (similarity, reflection), two (linear) or three (affine) with window sums in general position, so these classes need at least two, three and four blocks to identify the delay; (c) with known σ2\sigma^{2} and fixed designs, the expected log-likelihood gap of a wrong delay is at most the reliability-weighted energy of the lag-LL command changes 12​σ2​∑t∥M⁡(c¯t(d)−c¯t(d′))∥R~t−12\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\sum_{t}\lVert M(\bar{c}_{t}^{(d)}-\bar{c}_{t}^{(d^{\prime})})\rVert^{2}_{\tilde{R}_{t}^{-1}}.

Sketch.

A telescoping sum gives c¯t(d)−c¯t(d′)=∑j=dd′−1(cL​t+L−1−j−cL​t−1−j)\bar{c}_{t}^{(d)}-\bar{c}_{t}^{(d^{\prime})}=\sum_{j=d}^{d^{\prime}-1}(c_{Lt+L-1-j}-c_{Lt-1-j}), which gives (a). For (b), the designs are invertible at a nonzero window sum (Proposition B.1), so a map of the class reaches any target. For (c), take the projection onto the design of d′d^{\prime} in whitened coordinates, and bound the minimum over maps by the choice M′=MM^{\prime}=M. ∎

Proposition B.4 (Regret of the library against a label oracle).

Under T1–T4, for every sequence of readings, the cumulative log loss LAL_{A} of the predictive of the library satisfies

LA−Llabel′≤∑e=2Eln⁡1πe​(ze),L_{A}-L^{\prime}_{\text{label}}\leq\sum_{e=2}^{E}\ln\frac{1}{\pi_{e}(z_{e})}, (5)

where πe​(ze)\pi_{e}(z_{e}) is the prior mass of the source that holds the true hand. For a return after GG episodes to an entry with posterior mass r¯\bar{r} at its last visit, the use-count term ln⁡(∑j≠lastUj/Uze)\ln(\sum_{j\neq\text{last}}U_{j}/U_{z_{e}}) of Equation 4 is at most ln⁡11−γ+(G−1)​ln⁡1γ+ln⁡1r¯\ln\frac{1}{1-\gamma}+(G-1)\ln\frac{1}{\gamma}+\ln\frac{1}{\bar{r}} nats, with ln⁡11−γ=3.91\ln\frac{1}{1-\gamma}=3.91 and ln⁡1γ=0.020\ln\frac{1}{\gamma}=0.020.

Sketch.

Under T1 and T4, the score is the exact Bayes mixture over sources, so its loss in episode ee is −ln∑ℓπe(ℓ)Zℓ(𝒟e)≤−lnπe(ze)−lnZze(𝒟e)-\ln\sum_{\ell}\pi_{e}(\ell)Z_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}_{e})\leq-\ln\pi_{e}(z_{e})-\ln Z_{z_{e}}(\mathcal{D}_{e}). Under T2 and T3, the last term is the predictive of the oracle. For the return share, Uze≥γG​r¯U_{z_{e}}\geq\gamma^{G}\bar{r}, and each episode adds a mass of at most 1, so ∑jUj≤γ/(1−γ)\sum_{j}U_{j}\leq\gamma/(1-\gamma). ∎

This applies the analysis of Mixing Past Posteriors (Bousquet & Warmuth, 2002) to a hard-assignment library: the comparator pays the identification cost of each hand once, while a method that restarts from the prior pays it at every return. Fixed Share over the entries (Herbster & Warmuth, 1998) has the same form, with the cost ln⁡(Ke/α)\ln(K_{e}/\alpha) at each switch. Proposition B.4 holds exactly for a simplified library, with no capacity limit, merges, pruning or window test. It bounds the log loss of the readings, not the success of the planner.

Corollary B.5 (When the selection rule cannot matter).

Let two libraries share the sensor, the fits, the planner and their entries at the start of an episode, and differ only in the prior over sources. (a) Before the first reading, each plans with the mode of its prior, which is the last source when ρe<1/2\rho_{e}<1/2 (Fixed Share: when α<Ke/(Ke+1)\alpha<K_{e}/(K_{e}+1)). Both plan the first block of a switch with the previous hand. (b) Let ℓ∗\ell^{*} have the largest evidence, ℰ\mathcal{E} its log evidence margin over the other sources, and Λπ=maxℓ≠ℓ∗⁡ln⁡(π⁡(ℓ)/π⁡(ℓ∗))\Lambda_{\pi}=\max_{\ell\neq\ell^{*}}\ln(\pi(\ell)/\pi(\ell^{*})) its switch cost. If ℰ\mathcal{E} exceeds both switch costs, both libraries select ℓ∗\ell^{*}. (c) On the same randomness, the two libraries give the planner the same map until a block violates (b). A CUSUM rule with threshold cc satisfies the same statements, with the switch cost cc on its first informed block.

Sketch.

A library selects arg⁡maxℓ​[ln⁡π⁡(ℓ)+ln⁡Zℓ]\arg\max_{\ell}[\ln\pi(\ell)+\ln Z_{\ell}]. For ℓ≠ℓ∗\ell\neq\ell^{*}, the difference is at least ℰ−Λπ>0\mathcal{E}-\Lambda_{\pi}>0. Part (c) follows by induction over the blocks, because the map depends only on the entry and the readings. ∎

On our logs, the switch costs are a few nats (median 2.31 for the sticky prior, 2.5 for Fixed Share with three other sources, 3 for CUSUM), while the first reading of a return separates the hands by much more (tertile cuts 11 and 75 nats in the Gaussian scale). The corollary thus predicts a tie. With the same sensor, the sticky prior ties with Fixed Share (−0.9-0.9 [−2.7-2.7, +0.9+0.9]) and is 2.7 pp [0.9, 4.5] above CUSUM, so the prediction holds for Fixed Share but not fully for CUSUM.

Lemma B.6 (False alarms on the first block).

Let the identity be true, with Gaussian errors. Compare it with the similarity class on one block, with R~1=r​I\tilde{R}_{1}=rI and map prior precision λ0​I\lambda_{0}I, and let ψ=∥s1−c¯1∥2/r\psi=\lVert s_{1}-\bar{c}_{1}\rVert^{2}/r and κ=∥c¯1∥2/(r​λ0)\kappa=\lVert\bar{c}_{1}\rVert^{2}/(r\lambda_{0}). Then

ln⁡BF=(a0+1)​ln⁡b0+12​ψb0+12​ψ/(1+κ)−ln⁡(1+κ).\ln\mathrm{BF}=(a_{0}+1)\ln\frac{b_{0}+\frac{1}{2}\psi}{b_{0}+\frac{1}{2}\psi/(1+\kappa)}-\ln(1+\kappa). (6)

For prior odds OO and A=((1+κ)​O)1/(a0+1)<1+κA=((1+\kappa)O)^{1/(a_{0}+1)}<1+\kappa, the similarity model wins with probability exp(−x∗b0/σ2)\exp(-x^{*}b_{0}/\sigma^{2}), where x∗=(A−1)/(1−A/(1+κ))x^{*}=(A-1)/(1-A/(1+\kappa)). This grows with σ2/b0\sigma^{2}/b_{0} and tends to 1, so a noise prior far below the real noise causes false alarms.

Sketch.

The whitened design is (∥c¯1∥2/r)1/2(\lVert\bar{c}_{1}\rVert^{2}/r)^{1/2} times an orthogonal matrix, so the posterior and prior precisions satisfy detP1/detP0=(1+κ)2\det P_{1}/\det P_{0}=(1+\kappa)^{2}. The Woodbury identity gives RSS2=ψ/(1+κ)\mathrm{RSS}_{2}=\psi/(1+\kappa), and RSS1=ψ\mathrm{RSS}_{1}=\psi. Under A2, ψ/2​σ2\psi/2\sigma^{2} is a standard exponential variable, which gives the probability. ∎

Checks on the logs.

A script fixed the criteria of Table 10 before its first run. The checks use runs outside the locked test. Of 24 criteria, 16 hold on the final method (14 without the floor). The failures give three corrections. The noise prior sets the false-alarm rate of the first blocks (P5a, which led to Lemma B.6; this explanation is post hoc). The sensor errors are heavy-tailed, so the Fisher statements hold as orderings, not as calibrated numbers (P2a, P2b). The reliability also acts through contact, not only through the clip (P1d). We do not claim new regret bounds, the convergence of the fixed-point iteration of the clip model, or any bound on the success of the planner.

Appendix C Additional Results

All values are means over runs, and differences are in pp. Square brackets give the 95% percentile bootstrap CI of the mean over runs, not the range of the runs.

C.1 The locked test and the ablation per task

C.2 Further tests

Table 14 gives the tests that Section 4.7 and Section 6 summarise. Unless a row says otherwise, differences are LoH minus the named arm, and Appendix D gives the number of runs of each test.

C.3 Ablation: the floor

The floor makes a map admissible only if the smallest singular value of its linear part is at least 0.2, a value that we chose before any run (the weakest test hand has gain 0.5). The planner uses only admissible maps, and a segment whose best explanation is not admissible is not stored. Table 16 compares LoH with and without the floor. On the locked test, the floor changes success by +0.4+0.4 pp [−0.1-0.1, +0.9+0.9] over S1–S3, +0.1+0.1 [−0.9-0.9, +1.1+1.1] after returns and +0.1+0.1 [−0.3-0.3, +0.4+0.4] with no change. It matters in long runs. In the 500-episode streams of the JEPA-TTT protocol on PushT with no change, the AUC of LoH without the floor falls to 52.9, against 83.3 for the frozen planner. In a failed episode, some blocks show commands with almost no visible effect, so the library stores a map with a gain near zero (all such maps were below 0.08). A planner that uses this map sees almost no effect of any command, so CEM inflates the commands and the pusher leaves the image. The sensor then reads a constant, which confirms the map. With the floor, the AUC is 82.5.

Against a floor of 0.2, floors of 0.1, 0.3 and 0.4 change success after returns by −1.7-1.7 [−3.2-3.2, −0.3-0.3], +0.7+0.7 [−1.0-1.0, +2.5+2.5] and +0.2+0.2 pp [−1.1-1.1, +1.6+1.6] (post hoc).

C.4 Comparison with test-time training

We ran our re-implementations of JEPA-TTT (Zhang et al., 2026) and AdaJEPA (Wang et al., 2026b) on LeWM, on the protocol and the eight shifts of JEPA-TTT (Table 17). For each shift and seed, a stream of 500 episodes runs under one shift, and every 50 episodes, 100 held-out episodes start from a copy of each method. Best is the largest held-out success after at least 50 episodes, and AUC is the normalised area under the curve. The maps of LoH act on (x,y)(x,y), so it does not run on the two Cube shifts, which also change zz.

LoH wins when the command itself changes: a few blocks identify the map, while gradient steps on the weights need many episodes. It leads by 60.7 pp on the action rotation after 50 episodes. It loses on the two Two-Room shifts (−8.5-8.5 and −14.3-14.3 pp of AUC). There, the command turns by up to 75∘, with an angle that is a wave in the position of the agent, so the mean turn is close to zero. One map per hand can follow only this mean, while JEPA-TTT changes the model itself.

Table 18 gives the learned and calibration methods on our schedules. After returns, the three methods that adapt weights stay near the frozen planner (26.1 to 26.6%, against 26.1%).

Compute.

GPU time per environment step relative to the frozen planner, on the locked runs (PushT, Reacher, Two-Room), is 0.82, 0.78 and 0.82 for LoH, which makes 2.57, 2.44 and 1.54 plans per episode against 5.45, 5.29 and 3.25. With two and four times the CEM iterations, the frozen planner costs 1.91–2.03 and 3.59–4.18 times as much per step. Per plan, LoH costs 1.26 to 1.36 times a frozen plan (measured without the floor, which does not change the cost of a plan); it is cheaper per step because it replans about half as often.

C.5 RoboCasa: world models trained on real robot data

Set-up.

We use the three world models that Terver et al. (2025) pretrained on DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024) and their RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024) evaluation configurations, with the planner unchanged. The task is place in PnPCounterTop. Each episode has at most 60 planning steps, and one model action repeats for 5 environment steps. The hand acts on the xx and yy commands of the end-effector translation from the start of planning, so the set-up of the goal never sees it. The sensor inverts the planner’s own rollout, and a calibration of 8 episodes with no hand gives its R2R^{2}, gain and surprise threshold.

Rules fixed in advance.

A gate admits a model and a task only if the frozen planner with no hand succeeds at least 15 pp more often than under a turn of 90∘. It admits place for all three models. Reach fails the gate on DINO-WM and JEPA-WM, and the frozen V-JEPA 2-AC planner succeeds in none of 16 later episodes on it, so we do not run reach. Hand C does not lower the success of the frozen DINO-WM planner on place, so a rule fixed before the test replaces it with the first of B and E that costs 15 pp: E on DINO-WM and V-JEPA 2-AC, and B on JEPA-WM. The rules are P0, sensor R2R^{2} at least 0.5; P1, at least +10+10 over the frozen planner after returns on S1; and P2, at most 2 pp below it with no change. After returns are episodes 10, 11, 15, 16, 25, 26, 30 and 31. On V-JEPA 2-AC and JEPA-WM, four seeds were added after the reading of the first four, under a rule fixed before they ran that the 8-seed verdict replaces the first. On V-JEPA 2-AC, the first four seeds gave +28.1+28.1 [9.4, 43.8]; on the four added seeds, the frozen planner, LoH and the true hand all succeed in 25.0%, so these scenes leave no headroom.

The frame of the commands.

Each calibration map is turned by 22 to 39∘: the models read the RoboCasa commands in a turned frame. The sensor removes only the gain, so with no hand the library learns this turn as a hand. On S4, LoH plans with the identity in only 0–5% of its informed plans. This helps a little on DINO-WM and V-JEPA 2-AC and hurts on JEPA-WM, which agrees with the failure of P2 there but does not settle its cause: the calibration of JEPA-WM varies between runs (gain 0.73 and 0.94). The planner told the true hand removes only the injected hand, while LoH removes both the hand and this turn, so it can equal that planner (post hoc).

Recognition.

At the first informed plan of a return, LoH chooses the entry of the returning hand in 24, 17 and 21 of 64 returns on DINO-WM, JEPA-WM and V-JEPA 2-AC. It mostly learns a returning hand again. A fresh fit is confident by the second or third of 12 plans here, so recall saves little, and the lead over one memory is not significant on any model (post hoc).

A moved camera.

We moved the planner’s camera by a yaw θ\theta from −90∘-90^{\circ}{} to +90∘+90^{\circ}{} in steps of 30∘30^{\circ}{}, with no injected hand and the goal rendered by the same camera. The rules were fixed before the runs. K0: the sensor R2R^{2} is at least 0.5. K1: the slope of the turn on θ\theta lies in [−1.2,−0.3][-1.2,-0.3], with an interval that excludes 0. K1-DROID: this slope overlaps the slope of V-JEPA 2-AC on 261 DROID views, −0.67-0.67 [−0.81-0.81, −0.56-0.56]. K1 and K1-DROID pass on DINO-WM (−0.68-0.68 [−0.87-0.87, −0.47-0.47]) and V-JEPA 2-AC (−0.85-0.85 [−1.02-1.02, −0.65-0.65]). K1 fails on JEPA-WM (−0.32-0.32 [−1.01-1.01, +0.17+0.17]). Behind the robot, outside the DROID camera range, the sensor fails on all three models (Figure 7). A second stage measured the cost of the camera at the yaws where K0 passes. It is at least 15 pp (K2) only on V-JEPA 2-AC, and on the other two models a camera turned toward the DROID frame helps the frozen planner. We have not yet tested LoH with cameras that change and come back.

Appendix D Pre-registered Rules and Development History

Development history.

The method reached its final form in two steps. First, we adopted LoH without the floor, although its adoption rule failed on one of three criteria: the criterion of no loss under changes of the world failed on both seed sets. We adopted it because this loss has a separate cause (Section 6), and froze it before the locked test. Second, after the locked test, the 500-episode streams of the JEPA-TTT protocol showed a failure of this version (Section C.3), and we added the floor. Its pilot used 3 of the 20 locked-test seeds, and its confirmation used fresh seeds. On the 17 locked-test seeds that the pilot did not use, the locked rules give the same verdicts. Every result of LoH in the paper uses the final method, with the floor, unless it says otherwise; Table 16 gives LoH without the floor. Two other decisions did not follow a rule. A latent check to stop the world-change loss was designed, but a calibration showed that it could not separate false maps from new hands after one block, so we did not run its test. A calibrated noise prior was not adopted, because its gain did not replicate on fresh seeds (EBc1, EBc4).

Rules.

We wrote each rule below, with its bar, before the runs that it judges. Table 20 lists every rule on the final method, including the rules that fail. A bar applies to the estimate unless it says “CI”. “Ours” is LoH. nn counts runs, or seeds where marked s, or episodes where marked ep. TR is Two-Room. The rules on LoH without the floor give 47 passes, 10 failures and 4 rules that we did not run; the table repeats those whose verdict could change.
